title: Google Messages Nears Launch of RCS Video Calls, Boosting Android Messaging Experience
body:
Google is edging closer to bringing native video calling to its Messages app, a move that would finally unlock the long‑promised capabilities of the Rich Communication Services (RCS) standard for millions of Android users worldwide. While the feature is not yet ready for a public rollout, recent updates to the app’s codebase and new documentation from the GSMA point to a concerted effort by Google to integrate high‑definition, carrier‑agnostic video calls directly into text conversations. If successful, the addition could reshape the mobile messaging landscape by offering a seamless alternative to third‑party video platforms and further eroding the dominance of legacy SMS/MMS.

The RCS protocol, often billed as “SMS on steroids,” has been gradually evolving since its inception, adding features such as read receipts, typing indicators, and larger file transfers. Earlier this year, the GSMA announced that the next version of the specification would include native video call support, allowing carriers and device makers to embed real‑time video streams within chat threads without relying on separate apps. Google’s recent commit to the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) reveals that the company has begun laying the groundwork for this capability, adding new UI elements and signaling mechanisms that can negotiate video sessions over the RCS network. Although the code is still flagged as “experimental” and gated behind developer options, the presence of these components signals that Google is no longer merely testing the waters—it is building the plumbing needed for a full‑scale deployment.

For users, the impact would be immediate and tangible. Currently, Android users who wish to make video calls must switch to services like Google Meet, Zoom, or WhatsApp, each requiring its own app, account, and sometimes a data plan that bypasses carrier restrictions. A native RCS video call would allow a user to tap a camera icon inside a Messages thread, initiate a call, and have the video stream travel over the carrier’s own infrastructure, potentially reducing latency and improving quality for those on 4G or emerging 5G networks. Moreover, because RCS is designed to be interoperable across carriers, the experience could become universal, eliminating the fragmentation that still plagues many markets where only a subset of operators support advanced RCS features.

However, several hurdles remain before the promise can be realized. First, carrier adoption of the new RCS video specifications is uneven; while major operators in North America, Europe, and parts of Asia have already upgraded their core networks, many smaller or budget carriers have yet to implement the necessary software upgrades. Without widespread carrier support, the feature would be limited to a patchwork of users, undermining its appeal. Second, privacy and security considerations are paramount. Video calls carry sensitive visual data, and Google will need to ensure end‑to‑end encryption that meets both regulatory standards and consumer expectations. The company’s recent focus on privacy in its messaging suite suggests it is aware of these challenges, but concrete details have not yet been disclosed. Finally, competition from entrenched players such as Apple’s iMessage, which already offers seamless FaceTime integration, means Google must deliver a compelling, reliable experience to win over users accustomed to alternative ecosystems.

Industry analysts view Google’s push as part of a broader strategy to cement Android’s position as the default communications platform on smartphones. By consolidating chat, voice, and video into a single app, Google can collect richer interaction data, improve ad targeting, and strengthen its ecosystem of services. The move also aligns with the company’s recent investments in carrier‑grade technologies, such as the rollout of Project Fi’s 5G core and partnerships with telecoms to expand RCS coverage. If Google succeeds, it could accelerate the decline of legacy SMS and set a new baseline for mobile messaging that rivals the seamless integration seen in Apple’s ecosystem.

Looking ahead, the next few months will be critical. Developers are expected to receive further updates through the Android developer portal, and Google may begin limited field trials with select carriers to fine‑tune the video experience. Should these trials prove successful, a broader public launch could arrive as early as mid‑2025, coinciding with the wider rollout of 5G and the continued push for unified communication standards. For Android users, the prospect of native video calls embedded within everyday chats promises a more fluid, carrier‑independent way to stay connected—an evolution that could finally fulfill the original vision of RCS as the universal messaging protocol.
